vignette:
She is 61, married, and has spent most of her life working in agriculture, rising before dawn to tend fields, carry loads, weed, harvest, and do whatever the season demands. Her body has long been part of the work. She knows the weight of a bundle of greens, the sting of sun on her neck, the timing of planting by the smell of the soil. For many years, the rhythm of labor has given her a sense of purpose and a place in the family and community. That sense is shattered by a rape that occurs in a setting that should have been ordinary and safe, a moment that splits her life into before and after.

In the days immediately afterward, she moves through her duties in a kind of stunned obedience. She bathes repeatedly, scrubbing her skin until it reddens, as if she can erase what happened through force and repetition. She says little, even to her husband, and when he asks questions she turns away or changes the subject. She cannot bear to name the event aloud. Her silence is not calm; it is thick with shame and fear. She begins to feel that people can see something on her face, something damaged and exposed, even when she is dressed modestly and says nothing. The world feels altered. Paths she used to walk without thinking now seem dangerous. Men's voices make her stiffen. A hand reaching unexpectedly toward her causes her to flinch before she can stop herself.

As the weeks pass, sleep becomes one of the first things to break. She falls asleep exhausted, then wakes in the dark with her heart racing, her mouth dry, her body rigid as though she has heard someone in the room. Sometimes she wakes from dreams she cannot fully remember, only the feeling of being trapped and overpowered, the sense of her own helplessness returning with full force. On those mornings she lies still for a long time, staring at the ceiling or the woven pattern of the mosquito net, trying to gather herself enough to rise. When she does get up, she feels hollowed out and easily startled. A sudden shout from a neighbor, the slam of a metal gate, or the snap of a branch can send a jolt through her chest.

She keeps working because the household depends on her and because the field offers a structure she can still manage when everything else feels unstable. Yet even there, the work is changed. Tasks that used to be automatic now require concentration she does not always have. She forgets what she came to fetch, loses track of the sequence of chores, or stands motionless with tools in her hands, caught by a flash of memory she cannot control. Certain places near the edge of the field become impossible. If she sees a man standing alone on a path, her throat tightens and her body begins to shake. She starts to take longer routes, though they are tiring, and she times her movements so that she is never alone if she can help it. She becomes watchful in a way that feels endless, as if danger might return at any moment.

She also finds herself avoiding anything that might bring the assault back into her mind. She turns away from television scenes, from songs, from conversations about women being out after dark. When relatives ask why she no longer attends gatherings, she says she is tired or has work to do. Inside, she is managing a constant effort not to remember. Yet the memories find her anyway, often in fragments: the smell of sweat and dust, the pressure of being pinned, the terror in her own body. When they come, she feels helpless and angry at herself for not fighting harder, though she also knows, in another part of her, that survival was all she could manage.

Over time, she becomes less able to feel pleasure in the life she once had. Food tastes bland. Laughter in the courtyard seems distant. She continues to care for her family, but she does so with an effort that others may not fully notice. Her husband sees that she is changed and tries, in his own way, to protect her, but closeness is difficult. She wants comfort and recoils from touch at the same time. This contradiction leaves her feeling lonely even when she is not alone. There are days when her chest feels tight and her thoughts move in circles around what was taken from her. At other times she is irritable without knowing why, snapping at small things and then feeling ashamed.

Now, months and years later, she still lives with the event as if it remains present in the room beside her. She continues to fulfill her responsibilities, but the effort of doing so is constant, and her world remains narrowed by caution, silence, and the memory of violence that has not left her body.
